prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, reaching a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18 and opening new tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the clearest case on the shortlist of a new measurement capability that nature can check. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the Doppler, recoil and light-shift problems, and Ye's group brought systematic uncertainty and stability to the 10^-18 level. The consequences are concrete and easy to explain: a clock that notices a height difference of about a centimetre, laboratory tests of time dilation, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and the basis for a redefinition of the SI second. Independent laboratories reproduce the performance and compare clocks across sites, so the calibration and systematics work that I look for in an instrument result has been done by the community and not only by the discoverers. It also has by far the broadest support in our opening ballots: seven of eight members ranked it and four put it first, and all seven who named laureates proposed the same pair, so attribution is unusually clean.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the subject follows the 2005 prize for the frequency comb and the 2012 prize for ion-trap control and clocks, so some will call this a refinement of recognised work rather than a new discovery. A second point is timing: the SI second has not yet been redefined, and a two-person list leaves out other strong clock groups (for example in Paris, at NIST and in Germany) and the accelerating ytterbium and strontium comparison programmes. I also rely partly on recollection for exact priority of the early magic-wavelength experiments, and atomic physics is not my own field.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B001 first but flags that the committee may see it as a technological refinement of the 2005 comb and 2012 clock prizes, and that other clock groups could be argued as comparably decisive.
responses.response: I take the overlap concern seriously, but I read it differently. The comb was a tool and the 2012 prize was about controlling single quantum systems; neither delivered a many-atom clock whose systematics sit two orders of magnitude lower, which is what changed what can be measured, for instance gravitational redshift across millimetres. I agree the attribution to other groups is the real exposure, and I would want the citation worded around the lattice-clock concept and the 10^-18 demonstration so that it does not claim the whole field of optical clocks.

responses.point: Johansson puts B003 (circuit QED) first and B001 only fifth, while saying she defers to AMO and metrology colleagues, and she notes that circuit QED sits close to the 2025 prize and to her own collaborations.
responses.response: I respect that B003 is a clean piece of physics, and her openness about her ties to that community matters. But the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is close in subject and time, and circuit QED also has a real attribution problem: four credited names for three places, with Girvin or a theorist or experimentalist necessarily dropped. B001 has no such cut, so I would keep circuit QED as an alternative for a later year, not the first choice now. Her view that B001 is a distinct and decisive advance in precision measurement is, however, exactly what I would hope she can say in discussion.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B006 (defect-mediated 2D melting) first and B001 second, and asks whether the committee should wait for the SI second redefinition before rewarding the clocks.
responses.response: On timing I disagree. The prize is for the physics, which is confirmed by many labs, and not for a metrology decision that depends on international bodies and may take years; waiting makes the committee hostage to a process it does not control. On B006 I accept the elegance, and Mehlig is right that the hexatic phase is system dependent and some melting is first order, but with only one first-place vote and the Kosterlitz and Thouless overlap from 2016 I do not see it as a stronger candidate this year.

responses.point: Olsson puts B015 (room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance and MgO TMR) first, as the natural successor to the 2007 GMR prize with large technological impact in read heads and MRAM.
responses.response: The technological case for TMR is real and very mature, and I do not dismiss it. My difficulty is attribution: she herself points out that the MgO step is split between Parkin and groups not on the list, and Julliere's earlier result and the Butler and Mathon theory complicate the story. That uncertainty is not present for B001. I would be willing to see B015 discussed again if the committee can fix whether the prize is for the 1995 discovery or for MgO.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues in AMO (Lindroth, Kroll) judge Katori and Ye to be the decisive pair, and whether other lattice-clock groups should weigh more.
Whether the committee sees the 2005 and 2012 prizes as making optical lattice clocks a refinement and not a distinct discovery.
Whether a two-part prize should be considered, for example pairing B001 with a second achievement, since only two or three names are used.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B001, B042 or B003. I have no known personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or the circuit QED or cold-atom groups. For B045 and B002 my own fields (astroparticle and particle detectors) are adjacent, so I would be careful about weighting my own expertise there, and my PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations are not connected to the gamma-ray burst afterglow candidates as far as I know.
